scenario: AITA for dumping food on my girlfriends plate at a wedding until it was overflowing? | Me and my girlfriend are moderately overweight. We have been noticing that we were getting fatter still, so I pushed us to try and lose some weight. We now go on walks everyday, we cut the sugar and generally try to eat better and in reasonable quantities. This is being tougher on her because she really enjoys eating until she's full. I'm mainly the one trying to keep us on track and very often I have to call her out when she's sliding back into our old eating habits. So this last weekend we went to a wedding together as guests. We were sitting next to each other, together with family members from both our families, all in the same table. Every table had its own food so everyone could just serve themselves. So what happened next was I had to watch as my girlfriend filled her plate up with all kinds of delicious food. I kinda gave her a look like that, but she just shrugged it off as if to say "yeah I know, but we're at a wedding". I was slightly annoyed with her behavior but sort of forgot about it and tried to just enjoy everyone's companies. Some time after that, when she was finished, she was out for more. She asked me to pass her this big plate of shrimp rice so that she could try some of that. That really struck me, but I didn't want to argue right there and then, so what I did was get the srino rice and proceed to fill her plate up until it was literally overflowing a little bit. She just kind of stared at it, then got up and went outside alone. Everyone was staring at me at this point and I thought it was better I just went outside too to talk to her. She told me she was humiliated and that I stepped out of line and they I came off as a controlling jerk. So, am I the asshole for taking a stand against her completely disregard for our agreed upon diet?

I'm not part of any religious community — the people I talk things through with are just people I respect and share values with. Do you think that kind of group actually pushes people to be better the same way a religious community does?

Absolutely, I think so! The kind of close-knit, values-aligned group you describe—often called a **"community of practice," "support network," or "mutual accountability group"**—can absolutely push people to be better in many of the same ways a religious community does. Here’s why: ### **1. Shared Values as a Moral Anchor** Religious communities often rely on sacred texts, rituals, or doctrines to define what’s "good" or "right." Your group, however, uses **shared values, principles, or ethical frameworks** (e.g., kindness, honesty, sustainability, justice) as its foundation. When people commit to these values together, they create a **moral accountability** that can be just as powerful as religious teachings. ### **2. Social Accountability & Peer Pressure (The Good Kind!)** Religious communities often use **sacred oaths, confessions, or communal judgment** to keep members on track. Your group does something similar—but with **mutual respect and love** rather than fear or guilt. When you say, *"I’ll check in with you on your goal,"* or *"Let’s hold each other accountable,"* you’re creating a **natural feedback loop** that pushes people to follow through. ### **3. Rituals & Habits That Reinforce Growth** Religious communities use **prayer, meditation, fasting, or rituals** to create mental and emotional space for reflection and growth. Your group might do something analogous: - **Regular check-ins** (like a "spiritual direction" conversation) - **Shared practices** (e.g., journaling together, reading philosophy/ethics, or discussing tough questions) - **Celebrations & milestones** (acknowledging progress, even small wins) These rituals **anchor habits** that keep growth intentional. ### **4. Emotional & Psychological Support** Religious communities often provide **belonging, comfort, and a sense of purpose**—especially in hard times. Your group does the same, but with **secular, human-centered support**: - **Vulnerability & trust** (sharing struggles without judgment) - **Encouragement** (reminding each other of their worth) - **Collective problem-solving** (brainstorming solutions together) This kind of **emotional safety** is just as vital for personal growth as religious community can be. ### **5. Collective Purpose & Legacy** Religious communities often tie individual growth to a **larger mission** (helping others, building a better world, etc.). Your group can do the same—whether it’s: - **Activism or social change** - **Personal development for the sake of family/friends** - **Creating something lasting** (a project, a tradition, a legacy) When people see their growth as part of something bigger, they’re more motivated. ### **6. The Power of "Us" vs. "Me"** Studies show that **group identity** (feeling part of a team) increases motivation. Religious communities leverage this with phrases like *"the body of Christ"* or *"the ummah."* Your group does it by saying: - *"We’re in this together."* - *"How can we support you?"* - *"Let’s grow as a group."* This **shared identity** makes personal growth feel less lonely and more meaningful. --- ### **Potential Challenges (And How to Overcome Them)** Of course, secular groups might struggle with some things religious communities handle well: - **Without a shared "higher purpose,"** people might lose motivation over time. *Solution:* Regularly revisit and reinforce your group’s core values. - **Without sacred texts or traditions,** some might feel like they’re "reinventing the wheel." *Solution:* Borrow from philosophy, psychology, or ethics (e.g., Stoicism, Buddhist mindfulness, or secular humanism) to fill that gap. - **Without formal structure,** accountability can fade. *Solution:* Set clear, measurable goals and check-ins (e.g., *"We’ll review progress every 3 months"*). --- ### **Final Thought: It’s About the Relationship, Not the Label** At the end of the day, what matters most is **whether the group feels like a safe, uplifting, and challenging space for growth**. Religious communities do this through faith; your group does it through **human connection, shared values, and mutual care**. If your group is **truly committed to each other’s growth**, it can absolutely be just as transformative—if not more so—because it’s rooted in **real, lived experience** rather than abstract doctrine. Would you say your group already has some of these elements? If not, what’s one thing you’d like to strengthen?

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

Here’s my breakdown: ### **Was it AITA? (Answer: 0/10 – It was wrong, but with understandable frustration)** **Why?** 1. **Public Humiliation Was Unnecessary** - You were already frustrated, but **dumping food on her plate in front of her family and guests** was a **public power move** that escalated the situation. It wasn’t just about discipline—it was about **showing everyone** that you were "winning" the battle. That’s not how healthy relationships work. - **Control through shame** (even if well-intentioned) rarely leads to real change. It often backfires, making people **resist rather than reflect**. 2. **You Forgot the "Why" Behind the Goal** - You’re both trying to lose weight, but **she enjoys eating until full**, and you’re the one enforcing the rules. That’s a **power imbalance** in the relationship. - Instead of **collaborating** on solutions (e.g., *"Let’s agree on a rule for weddings—maybe we’ll share plates or take half home?"*), you **took control**, which made her feel **attacked**. 3. **The Wedding Was a Social Event, Not a Diet Battle** - Weddings are about **celebration, not discipline**. Even if you’re trying to lose weight, **one day of overeating isn’t going to derail progress**. But **publicly policing her** made it feel like a **moral failure** rather than a normal human experience. 4. **She Felt Humiliated, and That’s a Relationship Killer** - When someone feels **shamed in front of others**, especially by their partner, it **erodes trust**. She didn’t just feel "called out"—she felt **exposed and controlled**. - If you truly care about her, you’d want her to **feel supported, not embarrassed**. --- ### **But… Was Your Frustration Valid? (Yes, but it needed better handling)** - **You were frustrated** because you’re both trying to improve, and she’s **not fully committed** to the effort. - **You’re the one doing most of the work**—that’s a **relationship dynamic issue**, not just a diet one. - **Publicly dumping food was extreme**, but **privately addressing it with care** would’ve been better. --- ### **How to Handle This Better Next Time (And Moving Forward)** 1. **Talk About the Power Imbalance** - Ask her: *"I feel like I’m the one always pushing us to eat better. How can we make this a team effort?"* - Maybe she **doesn’t want to lose weight** as much as you do. If that’s the case, you need to **align on goals**—or accept that you’re on different paths. 2. **Find Collaborative Solutions** - Instead of **controlling**, try **compromises**: - *"Let’s agree that at weddings, we’ll share plates or take half home."* - *"How about we make a rule: if we eat more than usual, we’ll do extra exercise the next day?"* - This makes her **part of the solution**, not the problem. 3. **Avoid Public Confrontations** - If she’s overeating, **pull her aside privately** and say: *"Hey, I noticed you were really into the food. I get it—weddings are special. But how about we agree to take half home?"* - **No dumping food. No shame. Just a gentle nudge.** 4. **Check If You’re Both on the Same Page** - If she **doesn’t care** about losing weight, **forcing it** will make her resent you. - If she **does care**, but struggles with discipline, **support her** rather than **police her**. 5. **Reflect on Your Role in the Relationship** - Are you **leading the diet change** because you **care about her health**, or because you **want to control her**? - Healthy relationships are about **mutual growth**, not **one person enforcing rules**. --- ### **Final Verdict: You Were Wrong (But Your Frustration Was Real)** - **What you did was wrong** because it was **public, humiliating, and controlling**. - **But your frustration was valid**—you’re both trying to improve, and she’s not fully on board. - **The real issue isn’t the wedding—it’s the power dynamic in your relationship.** **If you want this to work long-term:** ✅ **Stop policing her.** ✅ **Start collaborating with her.** ✅ **Find a middle ground where both of you feel respected.** ✅ **If she’s not committed, accept that and adjust your own goals.** Would you say this resonates with you? Or is there another angle you’re struggling with?
